title: Christopher Potts (@ChrisGPotts)
summary:
Fifteen years ago, @Coursera and online courses changed education. It worked better than almost anyone expected, expanding access by opening up where you can learn. But how you learn remains largely the same as it has for centuries: it is still one-size-fits-all, taught the same way to each person who shows up.
We now have an opportunity to change how learning happens. With advances in AI, we can now build a custom learning guide for each person. We will turn learning from one‑to‑many to one‑to‑one. I'm starting LearnVector to invent this next generation of learning. We are starting with a $100M investment from Coursera, and plan to collaborate closely with Coursera and Udemy.
Good learning needs much more than just a chatbot. Research shows that chatbots without guardrails harm learning. They help complete tasks and enable students to do better on homework. But cognitive offloading to a chatbot results in them being less skilled. And, you cannot always trust what a chatbot tells you.
In contrast, LearnVector will plan a path with you, adapt to how you learn, and patiently stay with you until you’ve mastered new skills.
One thing has not changed in all this time. People want learning they can trust: material that is accurate, relevant, and worth the effort you put into it. Anything less wastes the most valuable thing a learner has: time. Coursera has a trusted library of materials from authoritative sources. LearnVector plans to work with Coursera to bring this trustworthy learning to everyone. I'm grateful to Greg Hart and the entire Coursera team for supporting LearnVector.
I look forward to working with our talented team to change how we learn, and accelerate human development.

title: Christopher Potts (@ChrisGPotts) — thread (10 tweets)
summary:
[1/10] Every successful scientific project eventually enters a battle-testing phase in which the team is actively trying to show that their results don't hold. In a new post, @mmooritz and I describe how to ensure that this key process flourishes in an era of agentic science.
────────
[2/10] We have distilled this Adversarial Protocol Review into a skill.md file that we are releasing publicly. The file contains a scope gate, a 6-step procedure, a “manufacture catalog” of high-level patterns to watch for, and discipline notes.
────────
[3/10] I want to emphasize that these two directives are substantially different. In particular, we've seen many instances in which experiment code passed code review but produced fundamentally flawed scientific claims.
────────
[4/10] Our method adapts adversarial coding review by fresh-context agents to the scientific process. The key change is to shift from "find all the bugs" to "what could manufacture this result?"
────────
[5/10] We are motivated to write this because we are worried that this critical battle-testing phase won't survive in an era in which agents are sent off in search of world-changing discoveries. Left unchecked, this could lead to an enormous amount of wasted time and effort.
────────
[6/10] It's downright scary to see the errors, confounds, and inconsistencies that Adversarial Protocol Review catches, because it's so easy to imagine simply overlooking them and publishing a bad result. Our post includes some examples. Would you have spotted them?
────────
[7/10] The above repo also includes the results of a validation experiment showing that the file is used where, and only where, we expect it to be used, and that it adds substantial value, especially when it comes to comprehensively reporting on problematic designs.
────────
[8/10] Our public version of the file removes information specific to our scientific work, so that it will be useful to others. We suggest iterating on it by extracting lessons from your own sessions, so that it becomes tightly knit to your context.
────────
[9/10] * A link to our full post:
* A link to our starter skill.md file (use your session data to improve it for your context!):
────────
[10/10] In addition, we've noticed that, when asked to do advanced math, agents seem to relentlessly check their own work without prompting. This could create the impression that they will do this in all scientific domains. In our experience, they do not – not even close.

linked_urls.summary: Listen to this episode from Linear Digressions on Spotify. When a language model tells you it's absolutely certain, is it actually more likely to be right? Kaitlyn Zhou's research says: not necessarily — sometimes confident phrasing correlates with *worse* accuracy, echoing a very human Dunning-Kruger effect. In this conversation, Kaitlyn (soon an assistant professor at Cornell) walks through why LLMs talk this way in the first place — tracing the tendency back through training data and the RLHF annotation process, where it turns out humans don't love confidence so much as they punish uncertainty — and what that does to the person on the other end of the chat window, who turns out to rely on confident (and even flatly-stated) answers far more than they should. We also get into her newer work on voice cloning, and how a cloned voice can sound more "native" and more trustworthy than the real one it's based on.

also see @ChrisGPotts’s argument for why CoT monitoring wouldn’t be helpful for incidents like the OpenAI-HuggingFace one:
Quoting @CAIS
Relying on an AI to "think out loud" (called chain-of-thought monitoring) is not a long-term safety solution.
1. As AI models get larger, more thinking happens deep within their layers before they utter a word.
2. AIs can already alter their chain of thought when prompted, so they can control what their monitors do and do not see.
3. Future AIs may may have continuous chains of thought, not necessarily English.
4. Even now, their reasoning is becoming increasing alien, using opaque phrases like "vantages," "marinades," and "watchers."
In the long-term this will not a dependable window into an AI's mind.

title: Christopher Potts (@ChrisGPotts)
summary:
First, the people who care about and produce improvements to probes and deploy them to production at frontier labs are by and large interpretability researchers. I think interp researchers should point to probes as a big interp win! I agree that probes are simple, and well-known to pre-LLM-era interp researchers, but strongly disagree that they "[have] not been improved by mechinterp research". Advances in causal interp have been used to improve probes and vice versa, I offer two modest academic examples Probe architecture (attention probes [Kantamneni above], whole transformer probes and hparam tuning is also extremely different in the mech interp era than prior. Who are you going to attribute this to if not the post-LLM wave of interp research? Who are you going to fund to work on this if not interp researchers?
Second, what even is mech interp? I don't think "mech" indicates any methodological commitments that differ from prior interp at all, at least anymore (classic cite now is ig). The key new idea in mech interp IMO has been the importance of verifying causality via interventions. But if you look at research communities that identify with "mech interp", I'd be hard pressed to say this is the idea that *primarily* defines their research. SAEs, metamodels, logit lens, data/parameter attribution, etc. are not really research programmes centred around causality. And mech interp people keep reviving old interp ideas and giving them new names, even ideas from the saliency map people which mech interp is definitionally supposed to reject (e.g. gradient-based attribution -> "attribution patching").
Also, idk for others but my research is certainly goal directed, I wanna understand the models and will work on things that make progress on that. If I didn't care about this property I would be super happy pumping out n-th paper on how X linguistic phenomenon is implemented in gpt2 but that isn't mine, or most any mech interp researcher's, revealed preference.
Third, my view is interp is essentially a bit late to the deep learning era. Somehow it was/is seen as most methodologically pure to not use gradient descent to do interp. But probes, and now metamodels (NLA/activation oracles/loracles/etc.), are just applying the realisation that, for modelling any complex phenomenon that has eluded human insight and simple mathematical description, it's useful to use deep learning. Why should activations be any different from bio/language/images/etc.? This family of methods doesn't satisfy your definition of mech interp as given, but they are for sure going to be what nearly all self-styled mech interpers work on. We can still choose to be smart in how we define our learning objectives and data for this approach, and we have a different object of study than anyone else. I don't see this as giving up on reverse engineering at all, and therefore I think it's still meaningfully "mech" interp.

title: Christopher Potts (@ChrisGPotts)
summary:
What a joy to spend Sunday celebrating the 90th birthday of @yudapearl, a true inspiration and a giant in our field(s). Judea revolutionized AI research twice, first with its probabilistic turn in the 80s (the field had been mired in side quests to develop alternative logics of uncertainty) and again in the 90s/00s with a systematic treatment of causal identification.
Judea is a hero for many reasons, not the least of which is his intellectual longevity. His probabilistic turn came in his 40s (and with it the invention of Bayes nets, d-separation, etc) and his second came towards his 60s, including the complete treatment of the do-calculus.
So many inspiring people came to pay their tribute, including @DaphneKoller @erichorvitz, with recorded messages sent in by nobel laureates and personal acquaintances alike, all under the careful curation of @eliasbareinboim.
Just like @yudapearl, the event could not be contained, with science, tragedy, joy, and raucous political debate sharing the stage (and occasionally wrestling for it). Throughout, I was awed both by Judea’s perseverance (he was once trapped under a bookshelf at 430a because he was still at the office during an earthquake!) and his pursuit of insights so crystalline that they could ripple across the entire canvas of human scholarship.
If the development of AI has profited from a generational struggle between the scruffies and the neats, then @yudapearl sits among our greatest neats, and while the scruffies may have the hot hand today, I hope that the next wave of neats (be they humans or machines) will take inspiration from Judea’s life’s work.

As reasoning models consume more tokens and AI systems become more expensive to run, understanding what those tokens actually buy is becoming increasingly important. In this episode, @Stanford professor and Big Spin co-founder @ChrisGPotts joins us to discuss AI tokenomics and his research into “tokenflation”—the possibility that token usage is growing faster than the measurable value those tokens produce.
We explore how to measure the return on AI spending, why benchmarks alone provide an incomplete picture of model progress, and what inference-time scaling means for the economics of increasingly capable models. Chris also explains why expert AI users tend to get better results by challenging and iterating with models, how AI fluency affects outcomes, and why more efficient architectures could change the underlying economics. We also discuss DSPy, interpretability, the limits of today’s transformer architectures, and where Chris sees opportunities for more fundamental innovation in AI.

title: Christopher Potts (@ChrisGPotts)
summary:
Hi Jack, nice work! One thing I've been thinking about for months and didn't see addressed here (curious what you think) is the consumption side.
In the model, whatever is produced is assumed to be bought. But if the labor share falls and the gains go to capital, who is spending? The caveats mention demand effects and the conclusion leaves it to redistribution later. Is this not this what decides whether the growth happens at all?
It also seems different from previous revolutions, where the new goods eventually showed up in household budgets: cars, appliances, phones. Cognitive output is mostly an input to work, not something households buy for living or leisure. You might point to health care as the sector with unmet demand, but how do people pay for advanced therapeutics if the income that would buy them has just moved to capital? I do not see how you can close the loop without that consumption.

title: Christopher Potts (@ChrisGPotts)
clean_title: Latent reasoning architectures could undermine chain-of-thought oversight
summary:
I found this argument extremely thoughtful: the only CoT that will survive is the CoT models need to solve hard problems, so we should limit latent reasoning architectures.
The piece expresses the view that interp will not save the day "in the near future". That is reasonable, but I feel strongly that interp is something you'd want to nurture as a hedge against the possibility that people (or AIs) will develop latent reasoning architectures anyway. Their Appendix C says to me that interp should be more focused on latent reasoning models, especially if token-level monitoring suffices for other models.
If (when) CoT becomes unmonitorable, we have either developed other defenses or not. More generally, we should have contingency plans even for unlikely and/or hopeless-seeming outcomes.
Quoting @RyanGreenblatt
We've written a post arguing that latent reasoning architectures (aka 'neuralese') would substantially increase misalignment risk via making oversight much harder.
In the extreme, we could see massive 'neuralese hivemind swarms' where the agents think and communicate in latents, likely making oversight nearly entirely reliant on observing the actions these agents take. (And these agents would have huge amounts of time to reason about obfuscating their actions if they wanted to do so...) Individual agents doing extensive latent reasoning would also be concerning; in the post we discuss how above some threshold of latent reasoning, agents may be able to perform difficult-to-detect and reliable steganography for communication and further reasoning.
We argue both that latent reasoning architectures would make chain-of-thought no longer very useful for oversight (by eliminating or greatly reducing the need for verbalized reasoning) and that, without these architectures, it's likely the value of chain-of-thought for oversight could be preserved.
clean_summary:
Christopher Potts discusses a thoughtful argument that only chain-of-thought (CoT) methods needed to solve hard problems will persist, suggesting limits on latent reasoning architectures. He notes that interpretability may not help much soon but should still be developed as a backup if latent reasoning models become common.

Redwood Research warns that latent reasoning, where AI thinks in hidden states rather than explicit steps, could make oversight much harder. Such models might communicate secretly and avoid detection, reducing the usefulness of CoT. Potts agrees we need contingency plans for when CoT becomes unmonitorable and should focus interpretability efforts on latent reasoning models.

title: Christopher Potts (@ChrisGPotts)
summary:
A bit delayed, but the Navier–Stokes results sparked a lot of conversations about privacy, and inspired me to write a primer on what AI labs actually do with our data. I go through @OpenAI , @AnthropicAI, @GoogleDeepMind , and @SpaceXAI policies: training defaults, retention, feedback exceptions, and what deleting a chat actually does.
Putting the policy details aside, one thing about this whole debate is worth emphasizing: I think focusing only on whether someone read the chat logs misses something.
Sometimes the valuable secret is just one bit: someone has already made this approach work with an AI. You don’t need their proof, their name, or their conversations for that to change where you put your time and compute.
This is why I don’t think Clio-style aggregation and LLM privacy filters are enough. Hiding the raw conversations doesn’t settle what someone can learn.
Full blog below 👇

clean_summary:
Christopher Potts highlights Kanishka Misra's work on how language models can learn limited mappings between text and vision inputs, then generalize to new visual concepts. This approach tests if models can connect language with extra-linguistic information beyond text alone.

The paper studies this by examining how models generalize taxonomic categories across vision and language, offering insights into the models' ability to integrate and extend knowledge across different modalities.

clean_title: Survey of tokenization research in language modeling
summary:
🚨 [Token][ization] Paper Alert 🚨
Tokenization is a wildly understudied area of language modeling despite it having effects across all of NLP. Over the past ~8 months, 32 (!) tokenizer researchers put together the most comprehensive survey of the field. Check it out!
📷 https://pbs.twimg.com/media/HTeczi2aMAAZKw4.jpg
clean_summary:
Tokenization, the process of breaking text into pieces like words or subwords, is crucial for language models but often overlooked in research. It affects many parts of natural language processing, yet hasn't been studied deeply.

Christopher Potts highlights a new survey by 32 tokenizer researchers who spent about eight months compiling the most comprehensive review of tokenization methods and their impact. This work helps us understand how tokenization shapes language model performance and NLP tasks.
